title: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
summary: Domain or tenant policy modification abuses the central control plane of a managed identity environment. Instead of attacking each machine, an adversary with delegated rights edits the settings that every machine or user obeys: Group Policy Objects in Active Directory, domain trust and federation configuration, or tenant settings in a cloud identity service. The direct cost of the edit is trivial, but the effect is multiplied because the setting is applied automatically and at scale. Changes are recorded as directory object modifications, policy file writes under the domain share, and cloud audit records of configuration calls. Defenders separate abuse from routine administration by looking at who made the change, from which host, outside of a change window, and whether the new setting produces a side effect such as a script or task running on many endpoints at once.

beginner.definition: This technique is about changing the central rules that a company uses to manage all its computers and accounts. In a Windows network those rules live in Group Policy. In cloud services the same idea appears as tenant settings. An attacker who can edit them can make every machine follow a new, harmful instruction.
beginner.whyItMatters: One small change at the centre can affect thousands of machines. An attacker does not need to break into each computer. They add a rule once, and the network applies it everywhere for them. These systems are also trusted, so their instructions usually run without question. If you do not watch who edits policy, a quiet change can look like normal administration until it causes damage.
howItWorks: The attacker gets an account with delegated rights over policy, usually through stolen credentials or privilege escalation.
They connect to the management console, the directory service, or the cloud administration interface.
They change or add a setting, such as a logon script, a task, or a trust link, and save it.
The environment distributes the new setting automatically to computers and users it applies to.
The setting runs on the targets, which may install tools, change permissions, or create new accounts.
Some attackers later revert the change so the visible configuration looks normal again.
beginner.example: Think of an apartment building where the manager keeps one master notice board for all residents. Adding a note to that board means every flat reads it that evening. An intruder who copies the manager key does not need to enter each flat. They just pin a notice telling everyone to leave a spare key outside the door. The harm came from one change to one shared board.
takeaways: Central policy systems are high value because one edit affects many systems.
Record which accounts can change policy, and review them often.
Compare policy changes with your approved change calendar to spot abuse.

objectives: Explain why central policy settings are valuable to an attacker.
Describe at least three examples of harmful policy changes and their effects.
Identify the log sources that record policy and tenant configuration changes.
Explain how to distinguish approved administration from malicious policy edits.
Describe how policy changes can be used for both persistence and privilege escalation.
Explain why a temporary change that is later reverted is hard to spot.
